name: Calliope Projects (B.W. Cooper) and No Limit Records
writeup: The B.W. Cooper public housing development, built between 1939 and 1941 and always called the Calliope, raised two generations of New Orleans musicians. The Neville brothers, pianist Willie Tee, the Dixie Cups and Henry Butler all lived here. Percy Miller, known as Master P, was raised in the Calliope by his grandparents, started No Limit Records in California, and moved the label to New Orleans around 1995. With his brothers C-Murder and Silkk the Shocker he made the project's name familiar to rap listeners nationwide, and No Limit sold more than fifty million albums by 2001. The complex flooded in 2005 and was fully demolished by 2014.

name: Club Rumors (Club Discovery)
writeup: This two-story building on St. Claude Avenue opened as the nightclub Club Discovery in 1988 and was renamed Club Rumors in 1993. It held a thousand people or more on weekend nights. When bounce appeared in 1991, the year used here, DJ Captain Charles broke the new records from its booth, and dance contests gave young performers a stage. KLC, who took over as DJ in 1993, tested his own productions on the crowd before Master P recruited him for No Limit; Mannie Fresh of Cash Money worked the same room. After shootings in 1997 the state revoked the club's license in 1998. The building still stands.

name: House of Dance and Feathers
writeup: Ronald W. Lewis, who had been involved with Mardi Gras Indians since he was thirteen, began this museum in his garage in the Lower Ninth Ward in 2003. It holds photographs and objects from Mardi Gras Indian gangs, social aid and pleasure club second lines and Skull and Bone gangs, all explained from inside the culture; Lewis was president of the Big Nine Social Aid and Pleasure Club. The first building flooded when the Industrial Canal levee failed in 2005, and a new one went up behind his house the next year. Lewis died of COVID-19 in March 2020. His wife, Minnie Lewis, reopened the museum in December 2022.

name: H&R Bar, Second and Dryades (site)
writeup: The H&R Bar, at the Central City corner of Second and Dryades streets, was the headquarters of the Wild Magnolias. Its hand-painted sign gave 1966 as the year it was established, two years after Bo Dollis became the gang's Big Chief. On Sunday evenings in the months before Carnival the Indians held practice inside, drumming and chanting. Dollis's voice caught the ear of Quint Davis, then a college student, which led to the 1970 single "Handa Wanda," with Willie Tee on keyboards and Snooks Eaglin on guitar behind the chant. Monk Boudreaux's Golden Eagles recorded the live album Lightning and Thunder in the bar in 1988. Fire destroyed it in 2001; the lot is empty.

name: Mount Moriah Baptist Church (Mahalia Jackson's church)
writeup: Mahalia Jackson, born in 1911 a few blocks away in the uptown riverside neighborhood now called the Black Pearl, learned to sing in this church. Her grandfather, Paul Clark, preached here from the 1910s. She stood out in the youth choir, moved up to the adult choir, and was baptized as a member in 1925, at fourteen. The congregation's "Dr. Watts" hymn singing and its foot-tapping, hand-clapping bounce shaped her style before she left for Chicago as a teenager. In 1956 she arranged a live national television broadcast of a Christmas service from the church, and her funeral procession passed it in 1972. The congregation still worships here.

name: Cosimo Recording Studios, Governor Nicholls Street
writeup: In 1956 Cosimo Matassa moved out of his J&M studio on North Rampart Street into a former warehouse on Governor Nicholls Street in the lower French Quarter, and renamed the business with what everyone already called it. Here a core of session players, among them saxophonists Lee Allen and Red Tyler, backed Fats Domino on "I'm Walkin'" and Little Richard on "Lucille." Huey "Piano" Smith's hits, Frankie Ford's "Sea Cruise," and Allen Toussaint's early productions followed, including Ernie K-Doe's "Mother-in-Law" and Chris Kenner's "I Like It Like That" in 1961. Around 1965 Matassa moved again, to Camp Street. The building survives in other use.

name: Ernie K-Doe's Mother-in-Law Lounge
writeup: Ernie K-Doe's "Mother-in-Law" topped the national pop and rhythm and blues charts in May 1961. By the 1980s he was better known in New Orleans for his outlandish, free-associating radio shows on WWOZ. In 1995 Antoinette Fox, whom he later married, opened this lounge on North Claiborne Avenue, and it gave the self-styled Emperor of the Universe a stage and a late revival. After he died on July 5, 2001, Antoinette kept it going, with a dressed mannequin of her husband on display, through the 2005 flood and until her own death on Mardi Gras Day 2009. The lounge closed in 2010. Trumpeter Kermit Ruffins reopened it in 2014.

name: Municipal Auditorium, New Orleans
writeup: The city's Municipal Auditorium opened in 1930 beside Congo Square as an opera house, concert hall, arena and Carnival ballroom in one. Its history tracks segregation in New Orleans music: there were protests over balcony access for Marian Anderson's concert in 1940, Louis Jordan called from the stage for an integrated audience in 1948, and the first integrated event came in 1953. Louis Armstrong, Mahalia Jackson, Fats Domino and Elvis Presley all played here. Ernie K-Doe battled James Brown in 1962, jazz festivals in 1968 and 1969 led to the first Jazz and Heritage Festival in 1970, and George Clinton premiered the Mothership in 1976. Damaged in the 2005 flood, it has stood vacant since.

name: The Ivanhoe, Bourbon Street
writeup: The Ivanhoe was a club at 601 Bourbon Street. In 1967 Art Neville's band, the Neville Sound, was pared down to become its house group: Neville on organ, Leo Nocentelli on guitar, George Porter Jr. on bass and Joseph "Zigaboo" Modeliste on drums. Playing six nights a week, the four tightened into a rhythm section and worked out long, spare instrumental grooves that won a local following. Allen Toussaint made them his studio band, and in 1969, renamed the Meters, they put their first four singles on the Hot 100, built from material developed at the Ivanhoe. The Radiators later traced their start to a 1971 jam session here. The building is now a different bar.

name: Candlelight Lounge
writeup: This barroom on North Robertson Street in Tremé was called the Grease Lounge in 1984, when a group of Clark High School students billed as the Rebirth Jazz Band made their first recording in it, a session organized by WWOZ co-founder Jerry Brock. Leona Grandison, known as Ms. Chine, and her brother Landry opened it as the Candlelight Lounge in 1985. The White Cloud Hunters held Indian practice here, and Sunday second lines stopped at the door. After the 2005 flood, when it was called the last live music room left in Tremé, Benny Jones brought his Treme Brass Band in on Wednesday nights, and it became the band's home base. Grandison died in 2020.

name: New Orleans Jazz Museum at the Old U.S. Mint
writeup: The New Orleans Jazz Club, founded in 1948, opened a jazz museum at 1017 Dumaine Street in 1961. It moved to the Royal Sonesta Hotel in 1969 and to Conti Street in 1973, then ran into money trouble and went into storage. On September 15, 1977, the start year used here, the whole collection was given to the Louisiana State Museum, which had just renovated the Old U.S. Mint on Esplanade Avenue; a jazz exhibit opened on the Mint's second floor in the early 1980s. The holdings include Louis Armstrong's first cornet, about 4,000 78 rpm records and more than 12,000 photographs. The building also has a performance hall on its third floor.

name: Buddy Bolden's House
writeup: Charles "Buddy" Bolden moved into this shotgun double on First Street in Central City in 1887, when he was ten, and lived here until 1906. These were the years in which he became the cornetist whom later players such as King Oliver and Louis Armstrong looked back to: his band came together around 1895, the start year used here, and worked Baptist church phrasing and dance hall blues into improvised dance music. After psychotic episodes and several arrests he was committed to the state hospital at Jackson in 1907 and died there in 1931. The house received landmark designation in 1978. A church bought it in 2008, and it has been cited for neglect since.
